It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: This cross-sectional study examined which interpretations of shared adversity were associated with solidarity across sectarian boundaries during the 2026 hostilities in Lebanon.

In a face-toface survey of 450 Lebanese adults (August 2026), we assessed common and intergroup threat, three formulations of inclusive victimhood, inter-sect contact, sectarianism, political interpretations, and hosting displaced people.
In preregistered adjusted models, common threat was positively associated with inter-sect solidarity, whereas inter-sect and displacement-related threat were negatively associated.

Common-humanity victimhood, which recognizes shared humanity despite differences in suffering, showed a substantial positive association with solidarity; beliefs that sects suffered equally showed no association.
Global victimhood similarity was positively associated only when examined separately from common-humanity victimhood.
Contact frequency and quality were positively associated with solidarity, whereas sectarianism was negatively associated; the hypothesized common-threat × sectarianism interaction was not supported.
Lebanon-Israel framing and having hosted displaced people were also positively associated with solidarity in their respective models.
In exploratory omnibus models, commonhumanity victimhood, contact, and displacement-related threat retained independent associations, but common threat, sectarianism, and war framing did not.

These correlational results distinguish recognizing shared vulnerability from perceiving other groups as threats and suggest that solidarity can coexist with recognition of different experiences of suffering.
War poses a dilemma for divided societies: common danger may encourage solidarity across group boundaries while intensifying mistrust between groups.
Social identity research links perceived common fate to mutual support (Drury, 2018), whereas intergroup threat research links perceived outgroup danger to unfavorable attitudes (Riek et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Social identity research links perceived common fate to mutual support <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Drury, 2018)</ref>, whereas intergroup threat research links perceived outgroup danger to unfavorable attitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Riek et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: The question is how people define who is threatened, interpret others' suffering, and determine whom to support.
We examine these distinctions in wartime Lebanon, where sectarian affiliation structures political representation and displacement creates demands for assistance across communities.
We define inter-sect solidarity as affective concern for members of other sects and intentions to assist them.
We distinguish perceived common threat from threats attributed to other communities, and recognition of shared victimhood from claims of equal suffering.
Contact, sectarianism, political interpretations, and hosting provide additional perspectives on solidarity's boundaries.
Lebanon's confessional power-sharing system embeds religious affiliation in political representation.
The 1943 National Pact established sect-based conventions for senior offices, while the 1989 Taif Agreement restructured power sharing following the 1975-1990 civil war (Haddad, 2001).
text.formatted: The 1943 National Pact established sect-based conventions for senior offices, while the 1989 Taif Agreement restructured power sharing following the 1975-1990 civil war <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Haddad, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: These arrangements have sustained sectarian categories as a basis of political competition (Delatolla, 2021).
text.formatted: These arrangements have sustained sectarian categories as a basis of political competition <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Delatolla, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: National belonging coexists with these divisions: studies in Lebanon have linked religious and national identifications to different orientations toward other sects and to divergent interpretations of civil-war victimization and responsibility (Licata et al., 2012; Zahreddine et al., 2026).
text.formatted: National belonging coexists with these divisions: studies in Lebanon have linked religious and national identifications to different orientations toward other sects and to divergent interpretations of civil-war victimization and responsibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Licata et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Zahreddine et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Hostilities involving Israel and Hezbollah since October 2023 escalated in 2024 and again in 2026, producing substantial displacement despite a November 2024 cessation-of-hostilities arrangement (Data Friendly Space, 2026; United Nations Security Council, 2026).
text.formatted: Hostilities involving Israel and Hezbollah since October 2023 escalated in 2024 and again in 2026, producing substantial displacement despite a November 2024 cessation-of-hostilities arrangement <ref type="bibr">(Data Friendly Space, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">United Nations Security Council, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: By mid-August 2026, approximately 352,000 people remained internally displaced, most outside collective shelters (United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs [OCHA], 2026).
Such circumstances make cooperation across sectarian boundaries consequential, while potentially heightening concerns over resources, security, and communal relations.
Shared emergencies may make broader social categories salient.

The social identity approach to emergencies links perceived common fate to shared identity and mutual support (Drury, 2018), while the common ingroup identity model suggests that inclusive categorization can reduce bias (Gaertner & Dovidio, 2000).
text.formatted: The social identity approach to emergencies links perceived common fate to shared identity and mutual support <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Drury, 2018)</ref>, while the common ingroup identity model suggests that inclusive categorization can reduce bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Gaertner & Dovidio, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Emphasizing Indian national identity experimentally increased Hindu participants' donations to Muslim beneficiaries (Charnysh et al., 2015), and inclusive identification strengthened solidarity with co-victimized workers (Subašić et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Emphasizing Indian national identity experimentally increased Hindu participants' donations to Muslim beneficiaries <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Charnysh et al., 2015)</ref>, and inclusive identification strengthened solidarity with co-victimized workers <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Subašić et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that perceived shared vulnerability may broaden concern, although exposure to the same danger does not necessarily produce a subjective sense of common fate.
The same conflict may also heighten concerns about other communities.

Perceived threats to resources, political influence, values, and identity are associated with less favorable outgroup attitudes (Riek et al., 2006); displacement can make resource competition and cultural change especially salient.
text.formatted: Perceived threats to resources, political influence, values, and identity are associated with less favorable outgroup attitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Riek et al., 2006)</ref>; displacement can make resource competition and cultural change especially salient.

text.text: Thus, perceiving a war as threatening all sects and perceiving other sects or displaced people as threatening one's own community are distinct appraisals that may relate to solidarity in opposite directions.
Sectarianism may further shape these associations.

Group attachment does not necessarily imply outgroup hostility: in Lebanon, sectarian collective narcissism was associated with support for collective violence whereas ordinary sectarian identification was not independently associated with it (Abou-Ismail et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Group attachment does not necessarily imply outgroup hostility: in Lebanon, sectarian collective narcissism was associated with support for collective violence whereas ordinary sectarian identification was not independently associated with it <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abou-Ismail et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, orientations that prioritize sectarian interests and advantage may restrict concern for other communities.
Sectarianism may therefore be negatively associated with inter-sect solidarity and may weaken the extent to which common threat corresponds to broader solidarity.
Beyond anticipating danger, people interpret how suffering is distributed across groups.

Inclusive victim consciousness recognizes connections between ingroup victimization and others' suffering (Vollhardt, 2015) and has been associated with support for refugees and immigrants and responsibility toward victims of violence (Vollhardt et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Inclusive victim consciousness recognizes connections between ingroup victimization and others' suffering <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Vollhardt, 2015)</ref> and has been associated with support for refugees and immigrants and responsibility toward victims of violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Vollhardt et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: A recent meta-analysis linked inclusive victimhood to less conflict-enhancing attitudes, in contrast with non-inclusive beliefs (Kljajić et al., 2026), while competitive victimhood has been associated with lower intergroup forgiveness (Noor et al., 2008).
text.formatted: A recent meta-analysis linked inclusive victimhood to less conflict-enhancing attitudes, in contrast with non-inclusive beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Kljajić et al., 2026)</ref>, while competitive victimhood has been associated with lower intergroup forgiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Noor et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Recognizing others' suffering does not require judging all groups' losses to be equal.
Inclusive narratives may acknowledge common experiences while preserving differences in severity, history, and recognition (Vollhardt et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Inclusive narratives may acknowledge common experiences while preserving differences in severity, history, and recognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Vollhardt et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Such acknowledgment matters to victimized groups (Bilali & Vollhardt, 2019).
text.formatted: Such acknowledgment matters to victimized groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bilali & Vollhardt, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Research on Lebanese civil-war memories likewise documented recognition of outgroup suffering alongside ingroup-centered responsibility attributions (Zahreddine et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Research on Lebanese civil-war memories likewise documented recognition of outgroup suffering alongside ingroup-centered responsibility attributions <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Zahreddine et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Recognizing another group as victimized is therefore conceptually distinct from asserting equivalence between its losses and one's own.
Inclusive victimhood also differs in its referent: perceived equality among local groups, parallels with victimized groups elsewhere, or common humanity despite differences in suffering.
General inclusive victimhood has been associated with willingness for some forms of contact with former adversaries in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Basque Country (Rupar et al., 2022).
text.formatted: General inclusive victimhood has been associated with willingness for some forms of contact with former adversaries in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Basque Country <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Rupar et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: We do not treat these formulations as established dimensions: each is represented by a theoretically motivated single item.
Their associations offer an initial comparison of equality, similarity, and recognition of difference as correlates of solidarity.
Intergroup contact offers a more interpersonal perspective.
Meta-analytic research links contact to reduced prejudice (Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006), including among individuals perceiving high intergroup threat (Van Assche et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Meta-analytic research links contact to reduced prejudice <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006)</ref>, including among individuals perceiving high intergroup threat <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Van Assche et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Frequency and quality nevertheless differ: negative encounters may be especially consequential for outgroup attitudes (Barlow et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Frequency and quality nevertheless differ: negative encounters may be especially consequential for outgroup attitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barlow et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In Lebanon, contact with Syrian refugees has been associated with more supportive hosting attitudes (Ghosn et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In Lebanon, contact with Syrian refugees has been associated with more supportive hosting attitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Ghosn et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Internal displacement may similarly combine opportunities for contact with practical assistance.
Political interpretations of war may also mark boundaries of collective concern.
A Lebanon-Israel framing may foreground the country as a shared political community, whereas an Israel-Hezbollah framing may emphasize a particular military and political actor.
The interpretations are not mutually exclusive, and neither measures national identification.
Research on inclusive categorization (Gaertner & Dovidio, 2000) suggests examining whether such understandings of the conflict's scope correspond to inter-sect solidarity.
text.formatted: Research on inclusive categorization <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Gaertner & Dovidio, 2000)</ref> suggests examining whether such understandings of the conflict's scope correspond to inter-sect solidarity.

text.text: We examined inter-sect solidarity in a cross-sectional, face-to-face survey of 450 Lebanese adults during the 2026 hostilities.
The outcome combines affective concern and intentions to help members of other sects; both components were also analyzed separately.
We distinguished common threat from inter-sect and displacement-related threats, and equal victimhood from global similarity and common-humanity victimhood.
We also examined contact, sectarianism, war interpretations, and hosting.
Because all measures were collected at one time point, the study tests associations rather than whether war increased solidarity.
The preregistered primary and secondary hypotheses concern associations rather than causal effects (Zahreddine, 2026).
text.formatted: The preregistered primary and secondary hypotheses concern associations rather than causal effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Zahreddine, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Perceiving the war as threatening all Lebanese sects will be positively associated with inter-sect solidarity.
Inter-sect threat (H2a) and displacement-related threat (H2b) will be negatively associated with solidarity.
Equal-victimhood beliefs (H3a), global victimhood similarity (H3b), and common-humanity victimhood (H3c) will each be positively associated with solidarity.
Contact frequency (H4a) and positive contact quality (H4b) will each be positively associated with solidarity.
Sectarianism will be negatively associated with solidarity.
Sectarianism will weaken the positive association between common threat and solidarity.
Endorsing a Lebanon-Israel interpretation will be positively associated with solidarity, whereas endorsing an Israel-Hezbollah interpretation will be negatively associated with solidarity.
Current and former hosts will report greater solidarity than nonhosts.
Among hosts, those who accommodated at least one person from another sect will report greater solidarity than those who hosted exclusively within their own sect (H8a).
Exploratory analyses examined war exposure, broader regional-conflict framing, and sectarianism as a moderator of inclusive-victimhood associations (Zahreddine, 2026).
text.formatted: Exploratory analyses examined war exposure, broader regional-conflict framing, and sectarianism as a moderator of inclusive-victimhood associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Zahreddine, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A cross-sectional survey of 450 Lebanese adults (18-73 years; M = 44.17, SD = 14.35; 50% women) was conducted by Information International from August 11 to 19, 2026.
Respondents were registered as Sunni Muslim (23.8%), Shia Muslim (24.0%), Druze (7.6%), or Christian (44.7%) and lived in Mount Lebanon (66.4%), Beirut (21.1%), or Saida city (12.4%).
They included currently displaced (7.6%), previously displaced (16.0%), and never-displaced (76.4%) participants (Table S1).
text.formatted: They included currently displaced (7.6%), previously displaced (16.0%), and never-displaced (76.4%) participants (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: Religious affiliation refers to the sect recorded in official civilregistry documents rather than an independently measured degree of religious identification.
Information International, a Lebanon-based survey research agency, administered the Arabic questionnaire face-to-face on tablets using 12 fieldworkers.
Fieldwork was restricted to Beirut, the Baabda, Metn, Aley, and Chouf districts of Mount Lebanon, and Saida city.

According to the agency's methodological report, interviews were allocated geographically using 2020 resident-population figures; neighborhoods were selected to reflect confessional diversity; households were selected systematically using estimated building counts; and an adult within each household was selected using a birthday procedure.
Of 638 households approached, 450 completed interviews, 178 refused, six were ineligible, and four were nonresponses after followup.
The agency's reported 71.7% participation rate is calculated as 450/(450 + 178), excluding ineligible and other nonresponse cases.
Because fieldwork areas were restricted and neighborhoods were selected partly to ensure confessional diversity, the sample is not nationally representative.
Eligible respondents were Lebanese citizens aged at least 18 residing in Lebanon.
Participation was voluntary, informed consent was obtained, and no directly identifying information was collected.
The University of Geneva approved the study (CUREG-2026-03-23).
text.formatted: The University of Geneva approved the study <ref type="bibr">(CUREG-2026-03-23)</ref>.

text.text: Sample size was primarily budget-constrained; a sensitivity analysis indicated approximately 80% power to detect an incremental effect of f² ≈ .018 (two-sided α = .05).
Unless otherwise specified, focal attitudinal and behavioral-intention items used fivepoint response scales, with higher scores indicating higher levels of the construct.
Responses of 'I do not know/have no opinion' (998) and 'Prefer not to answer' (999) were treated as missing.
Scores were calculated as item means under the completion rules in Table S2, which also reports reliability estimates.
text.formatted: Scores were calculated as item means under the completion rules in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S2</ref>, which also reports reliability estimates.

text.text: The questionnaire defines 'sect' using the Arabic term ṭāʾifa, referring to Lebanon's officially recognized religious sects, and the 'current war' as hostilities affecting Lebanon since 2024.
Background variables included age, gender, education, family-income adequacy, officially registered sect, and residence.
Displacement distinguished currently displaced, returned, and never-displaced respondents.
Hosting distinguished current, former, and neverhosts; the questionnaire defined hosting as providing displaced people with accommodation free of charge.
Among hosts, cross-sect hosting indicated whether at least one guest belonged to a different officially registered sect.
War exposure covered injury (participant or close family), bereavement, and damage to a residence (participant or close family).
These indicators were study-developed.
Two study-developed single items assessed common threat ("The current war poses a threat to all Lebanese religious sects") and direct threat to one's own sect.
Four inter-sect threat items covered cultural and value incompatibility, resource competition, and political influence (α = .67, ω = .69).
Two displacement-related threat items assessed resource competition/tensions and cultural change associated with displaced people from other sects (inter-item r = .62; Spearman-Brown = .76).
Inter-sect and displacement-related items were informed by realistic and symbolic intergroup threat measures (Stephan & Stephan, 2000; Stephan et al., 1998).
text.formatted: Inter-sect and displacement-related items were informed by realistic and symbolic intergroup threat measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Stephan & Stephan, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Stephan et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Six items assessed sectarian pride and attachment, perceived ability to serve Lebanon better than other sects, political consideration of sectarian interests, preferred government quotas, and sect superiority.
Five were adapted from Harb (2010); the superiority item followed Al-Amine et al. (2025).
text.formatted: Five were adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Harb (2010)</ref>; the superiority item followed Al-Amine et al. <ref type="bibr">(2025)</ref>.

text.text: Items were averaged (α = .78, ω = .79).
This composite therefore includes both identification-related items and positions concerning political advantage or superiority; it should not be interpreted as religious attachment alone.
Three study-developed agreement items assessed interpretations of the war as primarily between Israel and Hezbollah, between Lebanon and Israel, or as part of a broader regional conflict.
Participants could endorse multiple interpretations.
The three items were entered simultaneously in the confirmatory war-interpretation model; their separate associations should not be read as choices among mutually exclusive accounts.
Three single items assessed equal victimhood, global victimhood similarity, and common-humanity victimhood.
Equal victimhood asserted that harm to one's sect was 'neither less nor more severe' than harm to other sects.
Global similarity asked whether victimized groups worldwide had suffered in ways similar to one's sect.

Common humanity acknowledged 'essential differences' between groups' suffering while affirming, in the administered Arabic wording, that 'a victim remains a victim, whether from my sect or another sect.'
The global item was adapted from Vollhardt et al. (2016); the other items were developed with reference to inclusive victimhood research (Vollhardt, 2015; Vollhardt et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The global item was adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Vollhardt et al. (2016)</ref>; the other items were developed with reference to inclusive victimhood research <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Vollhardt, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Vollhardt et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The English reference questionnaire uses the phrase "whether here or there" for the final clause of the commonhumanity item.
These formulations are conceptually distinct single indicators, not established multi-item scales; their exact wording is documented in the questionnaire.
Contact frequency was assessed with one item asking how often participants interacted with members of other sects during the war (1 = Never,5 = Very often).
Those reporting contact also rated its overall valence (1 = Mostly positive,5 = Mostly negative), reverse-coded so higher scores indicated more positive contact.
The study-developed items reflected the frequencyquality distinction (Islam & Hewstone, 1993); contact quality was structurally missing for respondents reporting no contact.
text.formatted: The study-developed items reflected the frequencyquality distinction <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Islam & Hewstone, 1993)</ref>; contact quality was structurally missing for respondents reporting no contact.

text.text: Helping intentions comprised four items concerning practical assistance, donations, participation in community initiatives, and speaking out against unfair treatment of people from other sects (1 = Very unlikely,5 = Very likely; α = .84, ω = .85).
Affective solidarity comprised concern and empathy toward war-affected members of other sects (inter-item r = .75; Spearman-Brown = .86).
The items drew on work on outgroup solidarity, advocacy, and empathy (Glasford & Calcagno, 2012; Neufeld et al., 2019; Özkan et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The items drew on work on outgroup solidarity, advocacy, and empathy <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Glasford & Calcagno, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Neufeld et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Özkan et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The primary score averaged the two subscale means with equal weight.
Although the helping items concern possible actions, they measure self-reported intentions rather than observed behavior.
A separate study-developed item measured ingroup help prioritization and was excluded from the solidarity composite.
Preregistered hypotheses were tested in R 4.5.2 using multiple linear regression with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.
The threat dimensions and, separately, the three war interpretations were entered simultaneously; inclusive victimhood items were tested individually and jointly in a robustness model.
Contact quality was analysed among respondents reporting contact, adjusting for frequency.

For the common threat × sectarianism interaction, both predictors were centered around their respective means in the complete-case analytic sample; significant interactions were probed at -1 SD, the mean, and +1 SD of the moderator.

Confirmatory models adjusted for age, gender, education, economic situation, registered sect, residence, displacement, injury, bereavement, and property damage, except when a covariate was the focal predictor.
Models were repeated for helping intentions and affective solidarity separately.
Ingroup prioritization was examined using linear regression, with ordinal logistic regression as a sensitivity check.
All tests were two-tailed (α = .05).
Benjamini-Hochberg correction was applied separately to the 10 primary and four secondary directional hypothesis tests; support required the predicted coefficient direction and adjusted p < .05.
text.formatted: Benjamini-Hochberg correction was applied separately to the 10 primary and four secondary directional hypothesis tests; support required the predicted coefficient direction and adjusted p < .05.

text.text: Primary analyses used complete cases.

Where missing predictor or covariate data excluded over 5% of participants with observed outcomes, multiple imputation by chained equations (50 datasets) assessed robustness; structurally missing contact quality was not imputed.
Diagnostics included residual plots, variance inflation factors, and Cook's distance.
Exploratory analyses examined war exposure, sect-group differences, sectarianism as a moderator of inclusive-victimhood associations, and models entering multiple psychological predictors together.

The omnibus models included smaller complete-case samples than the preregistered models; differences between estimates are therefore descriptive and may reflect both added covariates and sample composition.
Additional psychometric, subgroup, and factor analyses are reported in the Supplementary Materials.
Confirmatory and exploratory findings were kept distinct.
Overall inter-sect solidarity was relatively high (M = 3.94, SD = 0.87).
Affective solidarity (M = 4.12, SD = 0.85) was somewhat higher than helping intentions (M = 3.74, SD = 1.03).
Common-humanity victimhood was also strongly endorsed (M = 4.28, SD = 0.87), whereas equal-victimhood beliefs were more moderate (M = 2.91, SD = 1.34).
Means, standard deviations, and Pearson zero-order correlations among the focal variables are presented in Table 1.

text.text: Threat Perceptions (H1, H2a, H2b)

In the model in which the four threat indicators were entered simultaneously, perceiving the war as a common threat to all Lebanese sects was associated with greater inter-sect solidarity, b = 0.123, 95% CI [0.064, 0.182], β = .203, pBH < .001, supporting H1.

text.text: We examined whether solidarity across Lebanon's politically salient sectarian boundaries differed according to interpretations of a shared wartime crisis.

In preregistered models, perceived common threat and common-humanity victimhood were positively associated with solidarity, while inter-sect and displacement-related threats were negatively associated; equal victimhood showed no association.
Exploratory omnibus models identified the most persistent independent associations for common-humanity victimhood, contact, and displacement-related threat.
These patterns do not demonstrate that war unified communities.
Instead, they distinguish appraisals of danger and suffering associated with concern and helping intentions in a divided political setting (Delatolla, 2021).
text.formatted: Instead, they distinguish appraisals of danger and suffering associated with concern and helping intentions in a divided political setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Delatolla, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Social identity accounts associate perceived common fate with shared identity and mutual support (Drury, 2018; Gaertner & Dovidio, 2000).
text.formatted: Social identity accounts associate perceived common fate with shared identity and mutual support <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Drury, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Gaertner & Dovidio, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this perspective, common threat was positively associated with solidarity in the preregistered threat model.
Yet inter-sect and displacement-related threats showed negative associations in the same model, whereas threat to one's own sect was not independently associated.

These contrasting findings suggest that the perceived scope and source of danger matter beyond a generalized sense of insecurity, connecting shared-fate accounts to intergroup threat research (Riek et al., 2006).
text.formatted: These contrasting findings suggest that the perceived scope and source of danger matter beyond a generalized sense of insecurity, connecting shared-fate accounts to intergroup threat research <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Riek et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Lebanon's sectarian political divisions (Delatolla, 2021) help explain why shared external danger may coexist with fears of competition over resources or assistance.
text.formatted: Lebanon's sectarian political divisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Delatolla, 2021)</ref> help explain why shared external danger may coexist with fears of competition over resources or assistance.

text.text: Respondents could perceive national vulnerability while anticipating disadvantages for their sect.

This possibility highlights the political interpretation of insecurity alongside its intensity, but the study did not measure national identification, shared-identity recategorization, or a causal sequence from threat to solidarity.
Research on co-victimization similarly suggests that shared exposure is not sufficient for solidarity without inclusive identity (Subašić et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Research on co-victimization similarly suggests that shared exposure is not sufficient for solidarity without inclusive identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Subašić et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, common threat was no longer independently associated with solidarity in exploratory omnibus models, whereas displacement-related threat remained negatively associated.
Because these models also used smaller complete-case samples, the attenuation cannot be attributed solely to the additional predictors.
The preregistered association should therefore not be interpreted as evidence of a stand-alone mechanism.
The victimhood findings distinguish perceived equality of suffering from recognition of shared humanity despite differences.
Inclusive victim consciousness has been associated with support for other victimized communities (Vollhardt, 2015; Vollhardt et al., 2016), but its formulations were not interchangeable here.
text.formatted: Inclusive victim consciousness has been associated with support for other victimized communities <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Vollhardt, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Vollhardt et al., 2016)</ref>, but its formulations were not interchangeable here.

text.text: Equal victimhood was unrelated to solidarity, while common-humanity victimhood remained strongly associated when the items were modeled jointly.
The common-humanity item explicitly acknowledged 'essential differences' in suffering.
This pattern is consistent with inclusiveness without presumed equivalence, but does not show that acknowledgment of inequality caused greater solidarity.
The two formulations also require different judgments: equal victimhood compares the severity of losses, while common humanity permits recognition without agreement on that comparison.
Lebanese civil-war research found recognition of outgroup victimization alongside group-centered attributions of responsibility (Zahreddine et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Lebanese civil-war research found recognition of outgroup victimization alongside group-centered attributions of responsibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Zahreddine et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings extend that question to contemporary solidarity, suggesting that concern for others may coexist with disagreement about relative suffering.
Respondents' reasons for endorsing either item, however, were not assessed.
Prior research emphasizes the importance of recognizing groups' particular experiences (Bilali & Vollhardt, 2019; Vollhardt et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Prior research emphasizes the importance of recognizing groups' particular experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bilali & Vollhardt, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Vollhardt et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A common-humanity formulation may preserve such recognition where an equality claim appears to flatten differences.
Yet we did not measure perceived acknowledgment, denial, or participants' interpretations of the wording.
The null equal-victimhood association therefore does not show that equality beliefs are harmful.
Future research should examine when recognition of shared experience is compatible with distinct historical and contemporary losses.
Global victimhood similarity was positively associated with solidarity in its separate preregistered model but not when all victimhood items were modeled jointly or in the exploratory omnibus.

Links between generalized inclusive victimhood and contact (Rupar et al., 2022), or victim-category accessibility (Sharvit & Kremer-Sharon, 2023), offer possible explanations that were not tested here.
text.formatted: Links between generalized inclusive victimhood and contact <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Rupar et al., 2022)</ref>, or victim-category accessibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Sharvit & Kremer-Sharon, 2023)</ref>, offer possible explanations that were not tested here.

text.text: Common-humanity responses may also overlap conceptually with compassion or universalistic concern, especially the empathy component of solidarity.
The association with helping intentions argues against a solely empathy-item association but does not establish discriminant validity or actual helping.
Experiments could vary recognition of different levels of harm independently of appeals to common humanity.
Contact frequency and positive quality were associated with solidarity and retained independent associations in the contact-subsample omnibus model.
These results extend contact research (Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006) to wartime concern and helping intentions.
text.formatted: These results extend contact research <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006)</ref> to wartime concern and helping intentions.

text.text: Positive contactattitude associations have also been documented under high perceived threat (Van Assche et al., 2023), but our study did not test threat as a moderator of contact.
Its contribution concerns a different outcome in a conflict setting, not evidence for that moderation process.
Contact during displacement may involve accommodation, work, or everyday encounters across sectarian boundaries.
Such interactions could personalize others' needs and complement common-humanity beliefs.
Nevertheless, independent associations do not demonstrate this sequence: respondents already inclined toward solidarity might seek more contact or perceive it more positively.
Frequency also need not imply cooperation, and negative contact can have especially adverse associations with attitudes (Barlow et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Frequency also need not imply cooperation, and negative contact can have especially adverse associations with attitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barlow et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Hosting was associated with greater solidarity, but selection into offering free accommodation may reflect prior concern, housing resources, or networks.
The cross-sect versus own-sect hosting comparison was imprecise (N = 62), so its null finding cannot establish equivalence.
Lebanese research on contact with Syrian refugees (Ghosn et al., 2019) and experimental contact evidence in another setting (Mousa, 2020) provide relevant, though not directly equivalent, context.
text.formatted: Lebanese research on contact with Syrian refugees <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Ghosn et al., 2019)</ref> and experimental contact evidence in another setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Mousa, 2020)</ref> provide relevant, though not directly equivalent, context.

text.text: Future research should distinguish who hosts, who is helped, the quality of interactions, and whether intentions translate into sustained assistance.
Sectarianism was negatively associated with solidarity in its separate adjusted model, but not independently associated in the exploratory omnibus.
The measure combined attachment with political advantage and superiority, and thus cannot isolate the role of religious identification.
Prior work distinguishes ordinary identification from collective narcissism (Abou-Ismail et al., 2023; Licata et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Prior work distinguishes ordinary identification from collective narcissism <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abou-Ismail et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Licata et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The unsupported common threat × sectarianism interaction likewise does not establish uniform associations across sectarianism levels.
More differentiated measures are needed.
A Lebanon-Israel interpretation was positively associated with solidarity, whereas the predicted negative association for an Israel-Hezbollah interpretation was not observed.
Both were entered in the same model; their differing significance does not establish a statistically tested difference.
National-identity salience experiments offer relevant context (Charnysh et al., 2015), but a war-framing item is not a measure of national identification.
text.formatted: National-identity salience experiments offer relevant context <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Charnysh et al., 2015)</ref>, but a war-framing item is not a measure of national identification.

text.text: Seeing Hezbollah as a combatant need not exclude concern for civilians.
This remains an interpretation of the null rather than evidence about respondents' political allegiances or reasoning.
Exploratory comparisons also caution against treating sectarian categories as fixed dispositions.
The broad Muslim comparison group included Sunni, Shia, and Druze respondents with heterogeneous patterns.
The common-humanity association differed between broad groups after multiplicity adjustment, but aggregation, restricted score variation, and untested measurement equivalence limit interpretation.
In Saida, relatively high mean solidarity cooccurred with higher ingroup prioritization at the group level; this does not demonstrate their coexistence within individuals.
These findings cannot establish intrinsic differences in generosity among religious communities.

Taken together, the findings suggest that solidarity in divided societies requires distinguishing shared vulnerability, perceived intergroup competition, equivalence of suffering, interpersonal connection, and political interpretation.
These are related orientations, not interchangeable signs of a unified response.

Inclusive identity theory suggests why broader categories may extend concern (Gaertner & Dovidio, 2000); inclusive-victimhood research highlights the importance of acknowledging particular experiences (Vollhardt, 2015); and contact research identifies interpersonal associations with more supportive relations (Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006).
text.formatted: Inclusive identity theory suggests why broader categories may extend concern <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Gaertner & Dovidio, 2000)</ref>; inclusive-victimhood research highlights the importance of acknowledging particular experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Vollhardt, 2015)</ref>; and contact research identifies interpersonal associations with more supportive relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Lebanon brings these processes into focus within an institutional order that sustains sectarian divisions while displacement creates needs across them.

In exploratory omnibus models, common-humanity victimhood, contact, and displacement-related threat showed the most persistent independent associations; preregistered associations for common threat, sectarianism, and war framing were more model-dependent.
The contribution is to clarify these distinctions, not to infer institutional reconciliation or political change from reported concern and intentions.

Displacement-related threat remained associated with solidarity in exploratory omnibus models, whereas exploratory income comparisons did not show a corresponding threat gradient; respondents whose income permitted saving reported lower solidarity.
Unadjusted comparisons also linked displacement and property damage with higher solidarity.
Thus, economic hardship should not automatically be equated with exclusion, nor do these findings establish that hardship promotes generosity.
Interventions could separately test material support for receiving communities, recognition of differentiated suffering, and opportunities for cooperative contact.
Their effectiveness is not demonstrated by this survey.
The cross-sectional design cannot establish whether threat appraisals, victimhood beliefs, and contact precede or follow solidarity.
Preregistration, covariate adjustment, robust standard errors, and multiple-imputation checks strengthen transparency, not causal identification.
The exploratory omnibus models also used smaller complete-case samples, so attenuation may reflect added predictors, sample composition, or both.
Fixed-sample nested-model comparisons and prospective designs are needed to clarify these differences; such nested comparisons are not reported here.
Most victimhood, framing, common-threat, and contact indicators were single items.
Inter-sect threat showed modest reliability, and sectarianism combined attachment with hierarchy-related orientations.
The common-humanity item may overlap with compassion or universalistic concern, particularly the empathy component of solidarity.
Associations with helping intentions do not establish discriminant validity, and neither outcome measures actual assistance.
Ceiling effects and social desirability may further shape responses.

Future work should use multi-item indicators, test discriminant validity and measurement invariance, include observed helping, and independently manipulate acknowledgment of unequal suffering and common humanity.
Generalization is limited by fieldwork in Beirut, selected districts of Mount Lebanon, and Saida city, with neighborhoods chosen partly for confessional diversity.
Systematic household and birthday-based respondent selection within these areas does not make the sample nationally representative.
Broad Christian-Muslim comparisons conceal sectarian heterogeneity, and the referent of 'other sects' differs across respondents.
Region, income, and exposure analyses are exploratory; the injury/bereavement subgroup had only 19 exposed participants.
Future studies should specify recipient groups, measure local resource and contact opportunities, and preregister adequately powered tests of group differences and moderation.
These cross-sectional findings do not establish that war increased solidarity.

In the sampled areas of Lebanon, common-humanity victimhood, inter-sect contact, and lower displacement-related threat showed the most consistent independent associations with affective concern and helping intentions in exploratory models.
Solidarity may therefore coexist with recognition of differences in groups' experiences of suffering rather than depend on claims of equal suffering.
Whether these orientations shape actual assistance and political cooperation requires longitudinal and experimental research.
